title: On-Camera Performance
article_body:
Most people who are uncomfortable on camera say the same thing: "I'm just not a natural." What they usually mean is that the first few videos they recorded felt awkward, and they concluded that the discomfort is permanent. It is not. On-camera performance is a skill, and like every skill, it improves with deliberate practice. The question is not whether your team can get good at it. The question is whether you give them the time, the repetition, and the right framework to do so.

The businesses that build a culture of camera confidence have a meaningful advantage. Buyers trust people more than brands. A salesperson who appears naturally and confidently on video — in a one-to-one email, in an educational article, in a product walkthrough — connects with prospects in a way that no written copy or designed graphic ever can. That connection is what moves deals.

## The SIMPLE On-Camera Framework

The SIMPLE framework gives your team a practical starting point for every video they record. Each letter addresses one of the most common on-camera mistakes and replaces it with a specific, actionable habit.

### S — Smile Before You Start

Most people look serious, flat, or slightly uncomfortable in the seconds before a video begins. That energy carries into the first words. Starting with a genuine smile — before the camera rolls, before the first word — resets the energy and signals warmth to the viewer. It feels unnatural at first. Do it anyway. Buyers respond to warmth.

### I — Imagine One Specific Person

Videos that try to address "everyone" end up connecting with no one. Before pressing record, picture a specific real person you are talking to — a real prospect, a real customer, someone who would genuinely benefit from this content. When you speak to one person in your mind, the delivery becomes more natural, more direct, and more personal. The viewer on the other end feels like you are talking to them specifically, because in a meaningful sense, you are.

### M — No Stop Rule

This is the rule that makes the biggest difference, fastest. When something goes wrong mid-video — a stumble, a pause, a sentence that doesn't land — the instinct is to stop and start over. Fight that instinct. Keep going. Push through. Stopping and restarting creates a loop where the discomfort never resolves because the person never finishes. When you push through imperfections, two things happen: you build the muscle memory to keep going under pressure, and you often discover that the video was far more watchable than you thought.

### P — Physical Presence

Stand up when possible. Standing activates your full range of physical expression — you can use your hands, shift your weight, and project energy that is simply not available when you are slumped in a chair. Good posture, whether standing or seated, communicates confidence. A camera positioned at eye level or slightly above works best. Looking down at a laptop camera adds unnecessary distortion and communicates the wrong power dynamic.

### L — Lead With Stories

Facts inform. Stories persuade. The most effective on-camera communicators do not recite information — they tell stories that carry the information. Instead of saying "our product reduces implementation time by 40%", say "one of our customers, a roofing company in Ohio, used to spend three days getting a new crew member trained. After working with us, that was down to a day and a half. Here's what changed for them." The same information, delivered as a story, is twice as memorable and twice as believable.

### E — Eye Contact With the Lens

Eye contact in video means looking at the camera lens, not at your own image on the screen. Looking at your face on a monitor while recording feels like eye contact to you, but it looks like avoidance to the viewer. The camera lens is the viewer's eyes. When you speak directly into it, the viewer experiences it as direct, confident eye contact. It takes adjustment. Mark the lens with a small sticker if that helps as a reminder until the habit is set.

## Preparation Without Scripts

Scripts kill natural delivery. When someone is reading from a script — even a memorized one — the viewer can feel it. The energy goes flat, the pacing becomes mechanical, and the connection disappears. The goal is not to memorize what you will say, but to know the core ideas well enough to speak to them naturally.

Before recording, write down three to five bullet points — the main ideas you want to cover, in order. Know where you are starting and where you are ending. Everything in between should be conversational. A brief outline gives you structure without trapping you in a script. If you need a reminder mid-video, look at your notes and then look back at the lens before speaking.

## How Leadership Shapes Camera Culture

Camera confidence is contagious — in both directions. When leadership never appears on camera, the implicit message to the team is that video is optional. When leaders go first, record consistently, and show their own imperfect progression, the team feels permission to do the same. Some of the most remarkable on-camera transformations happen not because of training but because a business owner put themselves on camera and the team watched them improve in real time.

Set a standard for volume and consistency, not perfection. A salesperson who records 100 videos in their first year will be dramatically more confident and effective on camera than the one who recorded 10 polished ones. Repetition is the only path to naturalness. Make that clear, model it yourself, and watch the team follow.

what_youll_learn: On-camera performance is a learnable skill, not an innate talent. Discomfort in early videos is normal and temporary — it resolves with repetition, not avoidance.
The SIMPLE framework gives your team six specific habits: Smile before starting, Imagine one person, No Stop Rule, Physical presence, Lead with stories, Eye contact with the lens.
The No Stop Rule is the most impactful single habit. Pushing through imperfections builds muscle memory faster than any amount of perfect retakes.
Scripts kill natural delivery. Prepare with three to five bullet points and speak conversationally — structure without imprisonment.
Eye contact in video means looking at the camera lens, not at your own image. That distinction is the difference between confident direct contact and avoidance.
Leadership behavior determines camera culture. When leaders go first and record consistently, the team follows. When leaders stay off camera, the team treats video as optional.

key_questions.question: How do we help a team member who is genuinely terrified of being on camera?
key_questions.answer: Start with low-stakes, low-visibility recordings. Have them record a short video that no one else will see — just to practice. Then a video for one internal colleague. Then a one-to-one prospect video that only one person will watch. The path from terror to confidence is always incremental. The No Stop Rule applies: keep going, do not restart, and review afterward. Most people discover their first complete video was far better than they expected.

key_questions.question: How long should on-camera training take before someone is ready to record for prospects?
key_questions.answer: There is no standard timeline, but a useful benchmark is 10 completed videos. Not 10 polished, perfect videos — 10 completed ones where the person finished regardless of how it felt. Most people find that by video 7 or 8, the physical discomfort has significantly reduced. The quality of the video matters less than the completion of it.

key_questions.question: Should on-camera videos be polished or can they be casual?
key_questions.answer: For one-to-one sales videos, casual and genuine almost always outperforms polished and produced. The point of a personal video email is human connection, and over-production works against that. For published educational content, a basic level of audio and lighting quality matters — but it does not require a studio. Good natural light, a quiet room, and a decent microphone are sufficient for most use cases.

key_questions.question: What equipment do team members need to start recording videos?
key_questions.answer: Less than most people think. A smartphone with a decent camera, a clip-on lapel microphone (available for under $30), and a window providing natural light is enough to record content that looks and sounds professional enough for buyer-facing use. The most common mistake is waiting until equipment is perfect. Start with what you have.

key_questions.question: How do we measure whether on-camera performance is improving?
key_questions.answer: Review early videos alongside more recent ones — the contrast is usually striking. More practically, measure response rates to one-to-one video emails versus text emails, and watch for buyer comments referencing the video. Prospects who feel a human connection before the first meeting will say so, and that feedback is the most direct signal that the investment is working.
